paragraphs: When men feel natural compassion for one another’s sufferings, when easy and frequent contact brings them together, and when no touchy feelings hold them apart, one may readily suppose that they will help one another whenever help is needed. When an American asks his fellow citizens for their cooperation, it is seldom refused, and I have often seen it given spontaneously and with great goodwill. If an accident happens on the highway, everyone hurries to help the victim. If some great and sudden calamity strikes a family, a thousand strangers willingly open their purses, and small but numerous gifts pour in to relieve the family’s distress. Among the most civilized nations of the world, it often happens that a poor wretch is as friendless in the midst of a crowd as the savage in his wilds. This is hardly ever the case in the United States. The Americans, who are always cold and often coarse in their manners, seldom show insensibility. If they do not eagerly offer their services, they do not refuse to give them.

None of this contradicts what I said earlier about individualism. The two things are so far from fighting each other that I can see how they agree. Equality of conditions, while it makes men feel their independence, shows them their own weakness. They are free but exposed to a thousand accidents, and experience soon teaches them that, although they do not habitually need the help of others, a time almost always comes when they cannot do without it. In Europe we constantly see men of the same profession ready to help one another. They are all exposed to the same ills, and that is enough to teach them to seek mutual protection, however hard-hearted and selfish they may otherwise be. When one of them falls into danger, and the others can save him by a slight, passing sacrifice or a sudden effort, they do not fail to try. It is not that they are deeply concerned about his fate. If their efforts happen to fail, they immediately forget what they were for and go back to their own business. But a kind of tacit and almost involuntary agreement has been made among them, by which each owes the others temporary support that he may in turn claim for himself. Extend to a whole people what is said here of a class, and you will understand my meaning. A similar covenant in fact exists among all the citizens of a democracy. They all feel subject to the same weakness and the same dangers, and their interest, as well as their sympathy, makes it a rule with them to lend each other help when it is needed. The more equal social conditions become, the more men show this reciprocal readiness to oblige one another. In democracies no great benefits are conferred, but good turns are constantly done. A man seldom shows self-devotion, but all men are ready to be of service to one another.
